title: The Web Origin Concept
summary: Defines the idea of an origin, used by browsers as the unit of authority and isolation, so content from one site cannot interfere with another. It explains how to work out the origin of a URI and write it as a string. It also defines the HTTP Origin header, which shows where a request came from.

eli5.summary: Each website lives in its own room, and browsers keep the rooms separate. This defines what counts as the same room, and the Origin label that says which room a request came from.

questions: what makes two urls same origin
subtitle: What a web origin is, how browsers compare it, and the HTTP Origin header that reports it.

tldr.problem: Browsers run content from many authors, some malicious, and need a consistent unit of trust so one site cannot disrupt another.
tldr.mechanism: An origin is the triple of scheme, host and port computed from a URI. Content from the same origin interacts freely; different origins are isolated. The Origin header tells servers which origins caused a request.
tldr.outcome: It gives a precise definition behind the same-origin policy, but the RFC admits origins are an imperfect, one-size-fits-all unit of isolation.

facts.label: Origin of a URI
facts.value: (scheme, host, port) triple, or a globally unique identifier

today: RFC 6454 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Browsers Need Origins
sections.content:
User agents handle content from many authors, and some might be malicious. Take an HTTP user agent that renders HTML and runs scripts: its implementor may want to stop a script from a malicious server from reading documents stored on an honest server, perhaps one behind a firewall.

Traditionally, user agents divide content by origin. Content from one origin may interact freely with other content from that origin, but how it interacts with content from another origin is restricted.

The RFC describes the principles of the same-origin policy and the mechanics of comparing and serializing origins. It does not describe every facet of the policy, leaving details to other specifications such as HTML and WebSockets (RFC 6455).
sections.eli5: A browser opens pages from lots of people, and some may be sneaky. So it keeps each website in its own box and only lets boxes talk in careful ways.

sections.title: Principles of the Same-Origin Policy
sections.content:
The policy is built on a few ideas. Trust is expressed by URI: a document that loads a script from a URI grants it the document's privileges, and a form that posts a password to a URI trusts the confidentiality of that destination. Protocol designers should make important trust distinctions visible in URIs. If TLS and non-TLS resources both used the http scheme, a document could not insist on TLS, which is why https is a separate scheme.

Origins group URIs. Treating every URI as its own protection domain would be cumbersome, so URIs with the same scheme, host and port form one origin. The scheme matters: without it, there would be no isolation between http://example.com and https://example.com, and an active network attacker could use the first to attack the second. The fully qualified host is used rather than just the top-level domain because trust varies by deployment. The RFC notes that this grouping is in some sense a historical artifact.

Authority differs by resource. An image is passive and carries no authority, while an HTML document carries the full authority of its origin. User agents decide this from the media type. Leaking an origin's authority to untrusted content is the vulnerability commonly known as cross-site scripting.
sections.eli5: Websites are told apart by three things: the kind of link (http or https), the name, and the door number. A picture is harmless, but a page with code in it is trusted with the whole room's keys.

sections.title: How Policy Applies
sections.content:
User agents isolate different origins and permit controlled communication between them. For objects (APIs), content from one URI can access objects of another URI only if both belong to the same origin. There are exceptions, such as parts of HTML's Location interface and postMessage, and exposing objects across origins is dangerous and should be done with great care.

For the network, reading information from another origin is generally forbidden. Still, an origin may execute script, render images and apply style sheets from any origin, and may display other origins' content in a frame. Resources can opt in to being read by other origins, for example with Cross-Origin Resource Sharing. Sending to another origin is permitted, but user agents restrict it to particular protocols, such as an HTTP request without custom headers.

The RFC warns about pitfalls: cross-origin interaction can leak image height and width, and sending requests gives rise to cross-site request forgery. It also advises granting privileges to whole origins, not to individual resources inside one, because resources in an origin are not isolated from each other.
sections.eli5: Pages can borrow pictures and scripts from other sites, but they cannot peek at what is inside another site's room unless that site says yes.

sections.title: Computing and Comparing Origins
sections.content:
The origin of a URI is computed by an algorithm. If the URI has no hierarchical naming authority, or is not absolute, the result is a fresh globally unique identifier. The same happens if the implementation does not support the scheme. For the file scheme, the implementation MAY return an implementation-defined value, and the RFC notes that a unique identifier for each file URI is the most secure option.

Otherwise the scheme is lowercased, the host is lowercased, and a missing port is replaced by the default port for the scheme. The result is the triple (scheme, host, port). The host is assumed to have already been through IDNA processing, so it holds only ASCII labels.

Two origins are the same if and only if they are identical: all three parts match for triples, and a unique identifier never equals a triple. So http://example.com/, http://example.com:80/ and http://example.com/path/file share an origin, while http://example.com:8080/, http://www.example.com/ and https://example.com/ each differ. A URI is not necessarily same-origin with itself: a data URI gets a unique identifier each time.
sections.eli5: To find a site's room, you write down the link type, the name and the door number. If two sites match on all three, they share a room. Some strange links get a brand-new secret room number every time.

sections.title: Serializing Origins
sections.content:
There are two ways to write an origin as a string. If the origin is not a scheme/host/port triple, both give the string null. Otherwise the result is the scheme, then ://, then the host, then a colon and the port in base ten only if the port differs from the scheme's default.

The Unicode serialization converts each A-label in the host to its U-label, joining components with full stops. The ASCII serialization uses the host as it is. The ASCII form is the one used in the Origin header.
sections.eli5: Writing a room down as text means joining the pieces like https://example.com. The door number is only added if it is not the usual one.

sections.title: The HTTP Origin Header Field
sections.content:
The Origin header field tells a server which origin or origins "caused" an HTTP request, as defined by the API that triggered it. For instance, a script run for one origin may cause a request, and the user agent MAY report that origin. If several origins contributed, such as one that issued the request and another that redirected it, the user agent MAY list them all.

The grammar is origin = "Origin:" OWS origin-list-or-null OWS, where the value is either null or a space-separated list of serialized origins. A user agent MAY include the header in any request but MUST NOT include more than one. From a privacy-sensitive context it MUST send the value null. Each serialized origin MUST be the ASCII serialization, and no two consecutive entries may be identical.
sections.eli5: The Origin header is a name tag the browser sticks on a request to say which website's room it came from. Sometimes the tag just says null, to keep the sender private.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The same-origin policy is a cornerstone of security for many user agents, but the origin is just a unit of isolation and imperfect, like most one-size-fits-all notions. The RFC lists systemic weaknesses.

  • Reliance on DNS. Schemes such as http depend on DNS, so a compromised DNS can defeat the policy. https is more resistant because of certificates, and isolating different schemes helps contain the damage.
  • Divergent units of isolation. Technologies such as cookies (RFC 6265) pre-date origins and use different boundaries. Using only the "registry-controlled" domain instead of the full host is NOT RECOMMENDED.
  • Ambient authority. Authority is granted by URI, not by which objects content can designate, which is why script injection is so damaging.
  • IDNA dependency. Moving between IDNA2003 and IDNA2008 can redraw security boundaries, even merging mutually distrusting entities into one origin.
sections.eli5: Room walls are only as good as the signs on the doors. If the naming system is tricked, or two systems draw walls in different places, sneaky sites can slip through.

viz.caption: SAME OR DIFFERENT ORIGIN, FROM RFC 6454 EXAMPLES

data.title: Origin header ABNF
data.code:
origin              = "Origin:" OWS origin-list-or-null OWS
origin-list-or-null = %x6E %x75 %x6C %x6C / origin-list
origin-list         = serialized-origin *( SP serialized-origin )
serialized-origin   = scheme "://" host [ ":" port ]
